dx: Bilateral ureteral obstruction from advanced cervical cancer with postrenal acute kidney injury
case: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because she has passed almost no urine for 24 hours. Eight months ago she was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and declined treatment. She has nausea and fatigue. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse 96/min, respirations 18/min, and blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a fixed, bulky cervical mass extending to both pelvic sidewalls. Bladder catheterization yields 25 mL of urine. Serum studies show urea nitrogen 78 mg/dL (7 to 20), creatinine 7.1 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), and potassium 6.1 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0). Ultrasonography shows bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter down to the level of the cervix. Diagnosis: postrenal acute kidney injury from bilateral ureteral obstruction by cervical cancer.

questions.stem: Bilateral percutaneous nephrostomy tubes are placed. Over the next 24 hours she produces 7.5 L of dilute urine. If these losses are not replaced, which of the following is most likely to develop?
options: Hypervolemia with hyperkalemia
Hypovolemia with hypokalemia
Hypervolemia with hyponatremia
Hypovolemia with hyperkalemia
approach: Recognize postobstructive diuresis: a large urine output after relief of bilateral obstruction.
Name its causes: excretion of retained urea and salt, plus injured tubules that cannot yet concentrate urine or reabsorb sodium normally.
Predict the losses: water, sodium, and potassium leave in large amounts, so volume depletion and hypokalemia follow without replacement.
questions.why: Bilateral obstruction stops urine flow from both kidneys, so creatinine, urea, potassium, and fluid build up and she becomes nearly anuric. Unilateral obstruction can stay silent because the other kidney compensates. When the obstruction is relieved, the retained solute causes an osmotic diuresis, and the injured tubules reabsorb sodium and water poorly and respond weakly to ADH. High flow through the distal nephron also increases potassium secretion. Without careful replacement she can become volume depleted and hypokalemic, so her earlier hyperkalemia swings the other way.
whyNot: Hypervolemia and hyperkalemia describe her state before relief, when no urine could leave. The diuresis removes both fluid and potassium.
Correct.
Hypervolemia with hyponatremia fits retained water, as in the obstructed state with ongoing water intake. After relief she loses large volumes of fluid.
Volume depletion is expected, but high distal flow increases potassium excretion, so potassium falls.

questions.stem: Which of the following anatomic relationships best explains how lateral spread of her tumor obstructed both ureters?
options: Each ureter runs within the round ligament to the deep inguinal ring
Each ureter crosses the external iliac artery near the inguinal ligament
Each ureter passes under the uterine artery beside the cervix
Each ureter descends behind the rectum in the presacral space
approach: Locate the tumor spread: the parametrium, the connective tissue at the base of the broad ligament beside the cervix.
Recall which structures run through the parametrium: the uterine artery and, just below it, the ureter on its way to the bladder.
Conclude that tumor in the parametrium encases both ureters at the same spot where a ureter can be tied during hysterectomy.
questions.why: After crossing the pelvic brim, each ureter runs down the lateral pelvic wall and then turns medially through the base of the broad ligament (the parametrium). There it passes under the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge") and continues past the lateral vaginal fornix to the bladder. Cervical cancer that spreads laterally into the parametrium encases the ureters here and causes hydronephrosis, a common cause of death in untreated disease. The same relationship puts the ureter at risk when the uterine artery is clamped during hysterectomy: ligation causes hydronephrosis, and transection causes a urine leak.
whyNot: The round ligament runs from the uterine horn to the deep inguinal ring and carries no ureter.
The ureter crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, near the common iliac bifurcation, far from the inguinal ligament and from parametrial tumor.
Correct.
The ureters lie on the lateral pelvic walls and never pass behind the rectum.

questions.stem: She later develops ascites containing malignant cells. When she is standing, fluid in her peritoneal cavity collects first in which of the following spaces?
options: Right paracolic gutter
Hepatorenal recess
Vesicouterine pouch
Rectouterine pouch
approach: Picture the peritoneum in a woman's pelvis: it drapes over the bladder, the uterus, and the rectum, forming two pouches.
Compare their depth: the rectouterine pouch reaches down to the posterior vaginal fornix, well below the vesicouterine pouch.
Conclude that the lowest peritoneal space in an upright woman is the rectouterine pouch.
questions.why: In women, peritoneum passes from the bladder onto the uterus, forming the shallow vesicouterine pouch, and from the uterus onto the rectum, forming the deeper rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas). In men, a single rectovesical pouch lies between bladder and rectum. The rectouterine pouch is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in an upright woman, so fluid, blood, pus, and shed tumor cells gather there. It lies right behind the posterior vaginal fornix, so it can be sampled through the vagina.
whyNot: The paracolic gutters carry fluid between the upper abdomen and the pelvis, but they lie higher than the pelvic pouches when she stands.
The hepatorenal recess is the lowest part of the abdominal cavity when a person lies supine. When upright, fluid runs down into the pelvis.
The vesicouterine pouch is a shallow space between the bladder and uterus. It sits higher than the rectouterine pouch.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before her ureters became blocked, Starling forces at her glomeruli were about: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure 60 mm Hg, Bowman space hydrostatic pressure 18 mm Hg, and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure 32 mm Hg. Obstruction raised Bowman space hydrostatic pressure to 26 mm Hg, with the other values unchanged. Bowman space oncotic pressure is negligible. Which of the following is closest to her net filtration pressure after obstruction?
options: 2 mm Hg
10 mm Hg
28 mm Hg
34 mm Hg
approach: Write the Starling equation: net filtration pressure equals glomerular hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman space hydrostatic pressure minus glomerular oncotic pressure (Bowman space oncotic pressure is about 0).
Before obstruction: 60 minus 18 minus 32 equals 10 mm Hg.
After obstruction: 60 minus 26 minus 32 equals 2 mm Hg, so GFR falls sharply.
questions.why: GFR equals the filtration coefficient times the net filtration pressure. Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, while Bowman space hydrostatic pressure and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure oppose it. Ureteral obstruction backs urine up into the tubules and Bowman space, so the opposing hydrostatic pressure rises and net filtration pressure drops from 10 to about 2 mm Hg. By contrast, hypoalbuminemia lowers glomerular oncotic pressure and tends to raise filtration, while dehydration lowers renal perfusion and glomerular hydrostatic pressure, so GFR falls.
whyNot: Correct.
10 mm Hg is her value before obstruction. It ignores the rise in Bowman space pressure.
28 mm Hg comes from subtracting only the glomerular oncotic pressure and leaving out Bowman space pressure.
34 mm Hg comes from subtracting only the new Bowman space pressure and leaving out the glomerular oncotic pressure.

dx: Acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy complicated by a perinephric abscess
case: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 24 weeks' gestation is admitted because of 2 days of fever, shaking chills, and right flank pain. Asymptomatic bacteriuria found at her first prenatal visit was not treated. Temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse 112/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 104/62 mm Hg. Right costovertebral angle tenderness is present. Leukocyte count is 18,500/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). Urinalysis shows numerous neutrophils and white blood cell casts. Urine culture grows more than 100,000 CFU/mL of an oxidase-negative, lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. After 72 hours of intravenous antibiotics she is still febrile, and ultrasonography shows a 5-cm fluid collection in the perirenal fat around the right kidney. Diagnosis: acute pyelonephritis complicated by a perinephric abscess.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the right kidney taken early in her illness would most likely show which of the following?
options: Eosinophils in the interstitium with tubulitis
Lymphocytes around atrophic tubules with colloid casts
Neutrophils in glomerular capillaries with subepithelial humps
Neutrophils in the interstitium and tubular lumens
approach: Connect the clues: fever, flank pain, and white cell casts mean bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma.
Recall the host response to acute bacterial infection: neutrophils recruited into the tissue.
Place them: in pyelonephritis neutrophils fill the interstitium and tubules, and the glomeruli are usually spared.
questions.why: Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation of the tubules and interstitium, usually from bacteria ascending from the bladder. Bacterial products draw neutrophils into the interstitium, and they spill into tubular lumens, where they are molded into white cell casts. Glomeruli are relatively resistant. Complications include papillary necrosis, pyonephrosis, sepsis, and, as here, a perinephric abscess when infection breaks through the renal capsule into the perirenal fat.
whyNot: Eosinophils with tubulitis suggest drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, a hypersensitivity reaction.
Lymphocytes with atrophic tubules full of colloid-like casts (thyroidization) describe chronic pyelonephritis after repeated infections.
Neutrophils in glomeruli with subepithelial humps describe poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which causes nephritic findings without flank pain or white cell casts.
Correct.

questions.stem: The organism isolated from her urine forms pink colonies on MacConkey agar. Which of the following was the most likely source of the bacteria that infected her urinary tract?
options: Her own colonic flora
Contaminated tap water
Her partner's urethral flora
Her own oropharyngeal flora
approach: Identify the organism: an oxidase-negative, lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod causing urinary infection is almost always Escherichia coli.
Recall where uropathogenic E. coli lives: the large intestine.
Trace the route: fecal bacteria colonize the perineum and periurethral area, then ascend the urethra to the bladder and kidney.
questions.why: Uropathogenic E. coli is the most common cause of cystitis and pyelonephritis. It comes from the patient's own fecal flora, colonizes the vaginal introitus and periurethral skin, and ascends into the bladder. Type 1 fimbriae help it bind the bladder lining, and P fimbriae help it bind the upper tract and cause pyelonephritis. Lactose fermentation gives pink colonies on MacConkey agar.
whyNot: Correct.
Water-borne gram-negative rods such as Pseudomonas do not ferment lactose and mainly cause urinary infection with catheters or instrumentation.
Intercourse can push bacteria into the urethra, but the bacteria themselves come from her own perineal and fecal flora.
Oral flora is mostly gram-positive and anaerobic organisms that rarely cause urinary infection.

questions.stem: Bacteriuria in pregnancy progresses to pyelonephritis more often than it does in women who are not pregnant. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: Loss of vaginal lactobacilli caused by high estrogen levels
Shortening of the urethra by the enlarging uterus
Ureteral dilation with slowed peristalsis and stasis
Suppression of neutrophil migration by placental hormones
approach: Note the clue: untreated bacteriuria early in pregnancy, followed by pyelonephritis.
Recall the urinary tract changes of pregnancy: progesterone relaxes ureteral smooth muscle, and the uterus compresses the ureters at the pelvic brim, more on the right.
Conclude that stasis in dilated ureters lets bladder bacteria ascend and multiply, so silent bacteriuria turns into pyelonephritis.
questions.why: Risk factors for cystitis include female sex, sexual intercourse, pregnancy, catheters, diabetes, and obstruction. In pregnancy, progesterone relaxes ureteral smooth muscle and the enlarging uterus presses on the ureters, so the collecting systems dilate and urine flows slowly. Stasis lets bacteria in the bladder ascend to the kidney. This is why pregnant women are screened for bacteriuria and treated even without symptoms. Cystitis alone causes dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic pain without fever, while pyelonephritis adds fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness, as in this patient.
whyNot: Estrogen supports vaginal lactobacilli, which acidify the vagina. High estrogen in pregnancy does not deplete them.
The urethra does not shorten in pregnancy. A short urethra explains why women in general get more urinary infections than men.
Correct.
Pregnancy shifts some immune responses, but neutrophil migration to the urinary tract stays intact. Mechanical stasis is the main reason.

questions.stem: Percutaneous drainage of the abscess is planned through the posterior flank. A needle passed above the 12th rib toward the upper pole of the right kidney is most likely to enter which of the following?
options: Hepatorenal recess of the peritoneum
Costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura
Descending (second) part of the duodenum
Right colic flexure
approach: Picture the kidney from behind: its upper pole lies against the diaphragm at the level of the 11th and 12th ribs.
Recall that the costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura extends down to about the 12th rib posteriorly, just behind the diaphragm.
Conclude that a posterior route above the 12th rib risks crossing the pleura and causing a pneumothorax or an infected pleural effusion.
questions.why: The kidneys lie on the posterior abdominal wall, with the upper poles against the diaphragm and the 11th and 12th ribs. Behind the diaphragm here is the costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura, which reaches the 12th rib posteriorly. This posterior position is why pyelonephritis causes costovertebral angle tenderness, and why posterior access above the 12th rib can puncture the pleura. A perinephric abscess sits in the perirenal fat inside the renal fascia, which keeps it near the kidney and can direct it downward toward the pelvis.
whyNot: The hepatorenal recess lies in front of the right kidney, between it and the liver. A posterior needle reaches the kidney before this peritoneal space.
Correct.
The descending duodenum lies anterior to the right renal hilum, so a posterior approach would have to pass through the kidney first.
The right colic flexure lies anterior to the lower pole of the right kidney, away from a needle aimed at the upper pole from behind.

dx: Genitourinary tuberculosis with sterile pyuria and ureteral stricture
case: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of 5 months of urinary frequency, burning on urination, and intermittent visible blood in the urine. He also reports night sweats and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. He moved to the United States 3 years ago from a country where tuberculosis is common. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). Urinalysis shows 35 WBC/hpf (0 to 5), 15 RBC/hpf (0 to 2), negative nitrite, and no organisms on Gram stain, and three routine urine cultures show no growth. Chest radiography shows calcified scarring at the right lung apex. CT urography shows irregular calyces in the left kidney, a stricture of the distal left ureter, and left hydronephrosis. Cultures of early-morning urine grow Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Diagnosis: genitourinary tuberculosis with ureteral stricture.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the organism most likely reached his kidney?
options: Hematogenous seeding from a lung infection
Ascent from the bladder along the ureteral lumen
Lymphatic spread from infected mediastinal nodes
Direct extension from an infected lumbar vertebra
approach: Link the clues: apical lung scarring and renal tuberculosis.
Recall that Mycobacterium tuberculosis reaches the kidney through the blood during primary or reactivated lung infection and seeds the well-perfused cortex.
Note that bladder and ureteral disease in tuberculosis come later, from bacilli shed downward from the kidney.
questions.why: Renal tuberculosis starts with hematogenous spread from the lungs, often years before symptoms. Bacilli lodge in the cortex and form caseating granulomas. These can erode into the calyces, and bacilli then pass down the ureter to the bladder, causing ulceration and fibrosis with strictures. Because routine cultures do not grow mycobacteria, the urine shows white cells without bacterial growth, called sterile pyuria.
whyNot: Correct.
Ascending infection is the usual route for E. coli. In tuberculosis the spread runs the other way, from the kidney down to the bladder.
Mediastinal nodes drain the lungs and do not drain toward the kidneys, so lymphatic spread does not explain renal seeding.
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) can track into the psoas, but it does not usually invade the kidney, and he has no back findings.

questions.stem: Before the mycobacterial cultures returned, chronic analgesic nephropathy was considered, because it can also cause sterile pyuria. In that disorder, which of the following sequences of injury is typical?
options: Glomerular sclerosis, then secondary tubular atrophy and fibrosis
Caseating cortical granulomas, then erosion into the calyces
Proximal tubular necrosis, then complete tubular regeneration
Papillary necrosis, then cortical interstitial nephritis
approach: Recall the setting: years of daily combination analgesics, classically aspirin with phenacetin or acetaminophen.
Recall where the drugs injure first: the papillae, where metabolites concentrate and blood flow depends on prostaglandins.
Conclude that papillary necrosis comes first, and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis in the overlying cortex follows.
questions.why: Chronic analgesic nephropathy follows long-term use of analgesic mixtures. The papillae are injured first, and the cortex above them then develops chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with atrophy and scarring. Sloughed papillae can cause hematuria, colic, or obstruction, and the urine often shows sterile pyuria. Other causes of papillary necrosis are diabetes, sickle cell disease or trait, severe acute pyelonephritis, and urinary obstruction.
whyNot: Glomerular sclerosis leading to tubular atrophy describes diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease, which starts in the glomeruli and vessels.
Caseating granulomas eroding into calyces describe renal tuberculosis, the diagnosis in this patient.
Tubular necrosis with regeneration follows acute ischemic or toxic injury, such as from aminoglycosides or contrast, not long-term analgesic use.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following functional abnormalities is most likely to appear first in his obstructed left kidney?
options: Loss of filtration barrier to plasma proteins
Impaired ability to concentrate urine
Reduced production of erythropoietin
Impaired 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D
approach: Recall what back pressure does in hydronephrosis: it is transmitted first to the papillae and inner medulla.
Note that the medullary vessels (vasa recta) are compressed, injuring the medullary tubules that build and use the concentration gradient.
Predict that the earliest defect is tubular, with poor urine concentration, before GFR falls and cortical atrophy appears.
questions.why: Persistent obstruction raises pressure in the pelvis and calyces. The pressure is transmitted back to the papillae and compresses the medullary blood vessels, so the medulla is injured first, and the earliest functional change is a loss of concentrating ability. With continued obstruction, GFR falls, the papillae become blunted and atrophic, and the cortex thins. Causes of hydronephrosis vary by age and sex: posterior urethral valves and ureteropelvic junction obstruction in children, stones and pregnancy in young adults, and prostatic enlargement and pelvic tumors in older adults.
whyNot: Obstruction does not damage the glomerular filter, so heavy proteinuria is not an early feature.
Correct.
Erythropoietin comes from cortical interstitial cells and falls only when much kidney mass is lost, and his other kidney compensates.
1-alpha-hydroxylation occurs in cortical proximal tubules and declines late, with loss of overall renal mass.

questions.stem: His stricture lies at the ureterovesical junction, one of the sites where stones also commonly lodge. Which of the following features of normal anatomy makes this one of the narrowest parts of the ureter?
options: Sharp bend where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels
Compression by gonadal vessels crossing anterior to it
Oblique course through the muscular bladder wall
Funnel-shaped junction with the renal pelvis
approach: Recall the three natural narrowings of the ureter: the ureteropelvic junction, the crossing of the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, and the ureterovesical junction.
Match the site: at the ureterovesical junction the ureter tunnels obliquely through the detrusor.
Conclude that this intramural segment is the narrowest part, where stones lodge and scarring easily blocks flow.
questions.why: Each ureter runs down on the psoas major, crosses the common iliac bifurcation at the pelvic brim, runs along the lateral pelvic wall, and enters the bladder obliquely through its wall. The intramural segment is the narrowest point, and the surrounding muscle also acts as a valve that prevents reflux. Stones commonly lodge at the ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim, and the ureterovesical junction. In tuberculosis, bacilli shed from the kidney inflame the ureter, and healing fibrosis produces strictures, often in the lower ureter.
whyNot: The bend over the iliac vessels narrows the ureter at the pelvic brim, a separate site higher up.
The gonadal vessels cross the ureter on the psoas in the abdomen, well above the bladder, and do not create a normal narrowing.
Correct.
The funnel-shaped ureteropelvic junction is the narrowing at the upper end of the ureter, at the kidney.

dx: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease with Potter sequence and congenital hepatic fibrosis
case: A male newborn delivered at 36 weeks' gestation is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for respiratory distress that began immediately after birth. Prenatal ultrasonography at 20 weeks showed severe oligohydramnios and bilaterally enlarged, echogenic kidneys. His parents are healthy and are first cousins. Examination shows a flattened nose, a recessed chin, low-set ears, bilateral clubfoot, and large, smooth masses filling both flanks. Chest radiography shows small lungs. Ultrasonography shows enlarged kidneys with many tiny cysts arranged radially from medulla to cortex, a small bladder, and increased echogenicity around the portal tracts of the liver. Serum creatinine on day 3 is 2.6 mg/dL (0.3 to 1.0). Diagnosis: autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease with Potter sequence and congenital hepatic fibrosis.

questions.stem: Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following correctly identifies the defective gene product and the risk that the parents' next child will be affected?
options: Polycystin-1; 50 percent
Polycystin-2; 50 percent
Fibrocystin; 25 percent
Fibrocystin; 50 percent
approach: Identify the inheritance: healthy, related parents and disease in a newborn point to autosomal recessive inheritance.
Name the gene: autosomal recessive PKD is caused by PKHD1 mutations, which encode fibrocystin, a ciliary protein.
Apply the recessive risk: two carrier parents have a 25 percent chance of an affected child with each pregnancy.
questions.why: Autosomal recessive PKD results from mutations in both copies of PKHD1 on chromosome 6, which encodes fibrocystin, a protein of the primary cilia of collecting duct and bile duct cells. Both parents are carriers, so each child has a 1 in 4 chance of being affected and a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier. Autosomal dominant PKD is caused by PKD1 (polycystin-1, chromosome 16) in most families or PKD2 (polycystin-2, chromosome 4) in the rest, and an affected parent passes it to half of the children.
whyNot: Polycystin-1 is the product of PKD1, the usual cause of autosomal dominant PKD, which needs an affected parent and usually presents in adults.
Polycystin-2 is the product of PKD2, a milder dominant form. A 50 percent risk applies when one parent is affected.
Correct.
Fibrocystin is the right protein, but a 50 percent risk fits dominant inheritance. Two carrier parents give a 25 percent risk.

questions.stem: His amniotic fluid volume was normal at 14 weeks but severely reduced at 20 weeks, a pattern also seen with bilateral renal agenesis. Which of the following best explains this timing?
options: Fetal swallowing of amniotic fluid begins
Fetal urine becomes the main source of amniotic fluid
Placental transfer of water to the amniotic cavity stops
Fetal lungs stop secreting fluid into the amniotic cavity
approach: Recall the sources of amniotic fluid: early on, mostly fluid crossing the fetal skin and membranes; from about 16 weeks, mostly fetal urine.
Apply it: kidneys that make little urine cannot maintain the fluid once urine becomes the main source.
Predict the Potter sequence: low fluid leads to compression of the fetus by the uterine wall and poor lung growth.
questions.why: In the first trimester, amniotic fluid comes largely from fluid crossing the fetal skin and membranes. Once the fetal kidneys are working, fetal urine becomes the main source, by about 16 weeks. Bilateral renal agenesis or severe bilateral kidney disease therefore causes oligohydramnios in the second trimester. The fetus is compressed by the uterine wall, producing a flattened face and limb deformities, and the lungs fail to grow (pulmonary hypoplasia). When only one kidney is missing, amniotic fluid stays normal and the remaining kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy.
whyNot: Fetal swallowing removes amniotic fluid rather than producing it, and it continues normally in this fetus. It does not explain the loss of fluid production.
Correct.
Water exchange across the placenta and membranes continues throughout pregnancy and does not stop at mid-gestation.
Fetal lungs secrete fluid throughout pregnancy, but lung fluid is a minor source compared with urine.

questions.stem: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, the form seen in adults, has extrarenal features that differ from those of his disorder. A 45-year-old man with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease has a midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the cardiac apex. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this finding?
options: Myxomatous mitral valve degeneration
Rheumatic fusion of the mitral commissures
Calcific degeneration of the aortic valve
Congenital bicuspid aortic valve
approach: Interpret the sound: a midsystolic click with a late systolic murmur at the apex is mitral valve prolapse.
Recall the extrarenal features of autosomal dominant PKD: liver cysts, berry aneurysms, and mitral valve prolapse.
Recall the lesion behind prolapse: myxomatous degeneration of the mitral leaflets.
questions.why: Autosomal dominant PKD presents in adults with bilaterally enlarged cystic kidneys, flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, and slowly progressive renal failure. Extrarenal features include liver cysts, berry aneurysms that can rupture and cause subarachnoid hemorrhage, and mitral valve prolapse. Mitral valve prolapse is caused by myxomatous degeneration of the leaflets, which balloon back into the atrium in mid systole and produce a click. In the recessive infantile form, the liver lesion is congenital hepatic fibrosis instead of cysts.
whyNot: Correct.
Rheumatic fusion of the commissures causes mitral stenosis, heard as an opening snap and a diastolic rumble.
Calcific aortic stenosis causes a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, usually in older adults.
A bicuspid aortic valve can cause an early ejection click at the base and is not a feature of autosomal dominant PKD.

topics: Extrarenal features of autosomal dominant PKD

questions.stem: Which of the following prenatal ultrasound findings, if present, would instead have pointed to posterior urethral valves as the cause of his oligohydramnios?
options: Enlarged echogenic kidneys with a small bladder
Absent kidneys with an empty renal fossa on each side
A unilateral multicystic kidney with normal fluid
Bilateral hydronephrosis with a distended bladder
approach: Locate the obstruction: posterior urethral valves block the urethra below the bladder in male fetuses.
Predict the upstream effects: the bladder fills and thickens, and both ureters and kidneys dilate.
Compare with this infant: enlarged echogenic kidneys and a small bladder point to kidneys that make little urine.
questions.why: Posterior urethral valves are folds of tissue in the prostatic urethra of male fetuses that block urine outflow. Because the block is below the bladder, the bladder becomes distended and thick-walled, the posterior urethra dilates, and back pressure causes bilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis. Little urine reaches the amniotic cavity, so oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia can follow. In this infant the kidneys themselves made little urine, so the bladder stayed small.
whyNot: Enlarged echogenic kidneys with a small bladder describe this infant's recessive polycystic disease, where the kidneys make little urine.
Absent kidneys on both sides describe bilateral renal agenesis.
A unilateral multicystic dysplastic kidney leaves the other kidney working, so amniotic fluid stays normal.
Correct.

dx: Ectopic pelvic kidney with primary vesicoureteral reflux and renal scarring in a school-age girl
case: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician after her third febrile urinary tract infection in 2 years. Each episode grew Escherichia coli. Temperature today is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Ultrasonography shows a right kidney in the normal lumbar position and a small left kidney lying in the pelvis, anterior to the sacrum, with an irregular outline. A renal cortical scan shows two focal scars in the left kidney. A voiding cystourethrogram shows contrast refluxing up the left ureter into a dilated renal pelvis during voiding. Serum creatinine is 0.5 mg/dL (0.3 to 0.7). Diagnosis: ectopic pelvic left kidney with primary vesicoureteral reflux and reflux nephropathy.

questions.stem: Angiography before surgery is most likely to show that her left kidney receives its blood supply from which of the following?
options: A single renal artery from the aorta at the L1 to L2 level
Vessels from the distal aorta or iliac arteries
Branches of the superior mesenteric artery
Branches of the inferior epigastric artery
approach: Recall normal ascent: the metanephric kidneys form in the pelvis and rise to the lumbar region between about weeks 6 and 9.
Recall that during ascent each kidney gets new arteries from successively higher levels of the aorta, and the lower ones regress.
Apply it: a kidney that stays in the pelvis keeps its early supply from the distal aorta or iliac arteries.
questions.why: The permanent kidneys begin in the pelvis and ascend to the posterior abdominal wall, largely because the body grows away from them. As they rise, they are supplied by a series of arteries from progressively higher levels, and the lower vessels usually disappear. A kidney that fails to ascend remains in the pelvis, supplied by nearby vessels such as the common iliac artery or the lower aorta. When the lower poles fuse, the resulting horseshoe kidney is trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery. Persistent lower vessels also explain accessory renal arteries in normally placed kidneys.
whyNot: A single renal artery at L1 to L2 is the normal pattern for a kidney that completed its ascent to the lumbar region.
Correct.
The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut bowel and does not give branches to the developing kidneys.
The inferior epigastric artery runs in the anterior abdominal wall and does not supply the kidneys.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why urine refluxes into her left ureter during voiding?
options: Obstruction of the bladder outlet by urethral valves
Detrusor overactivity from a spinal cord lesion
Stricture at the left ureteropelvic junction
A short intramural ureteral segment
approach: Recall the antireflux valve: the ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall, and bladder pressure during voiding squeezes this segment shut.
Recognize primary reflux: in a girl with no outlet obstruction or neurologic disease, the usual cause is a congenitally short intravesical segment.
Predict the result: infected urine reaches the kidney, causing recurrent pyelonephritis and scarring (reflux nephropathy).
questions.why: Normally the ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall for some distance before it opens. When the bladder contracts, pressure flattens this segment and it acts as a flap valve. In primary vesicoureteral reflux, the intravesical segment is short and the orifice sits laterally, so the valve fails and urine flows back up the ureter during voiding. Bacteria from the bladder then reach the kidney, causing recurrent pyelonephritis and cortical scarring. The voiding cystourethrogram is the study that shows reflux.
whyNot: Urethral valves cause secondary reflux in boys, with a distended, thick-walled bladder. She has no outlet obstruction.
High bladder pressure from a neurogenic bladder can cause secondary reflux, but she has no neurologic disease. Her reflux is primary.
A ureteropelvic junction stricture blocks flow from the pelvis into the ureter. It causes hydronephrosis without reflux of contrast from the bladder.
Correct.

questions.stem: If her reflux and infections continue, gross examination of the left kidney years later would most likely show which of the following?
options: Symmetric shrinkage with a finely granular surface
Pinpoint hemorrhages giving a flea-bitten surface
Coarse irregular scars over blunted calyces
Diffuse enlargement with a pale, smooth cortex
approach: Recall that reflux carries bacteria into the papillae and up into the renal parenchyma.
Picture repeated infection: each episode destroys a segment of medulla and cortex and leaves a deep scar.
Conclude: chronic pyelonephritis gives coarse, irregular scars over blunted, deformed calyces, unlike the even changes of vascular disease.
questions.why: Chronic pyelonephritis from reflux or obstruction produces irregular, asymmetric kidneys with coarse corticomedullary scars. Each scar lies over a blunted or deformed calyx, because the infection damages the papilla and the cortex above it. Microscopically, tubules are atrophic or dilated and filled with eosinophilic casts that resemble thyroid colloid (thyroidization), with chronic interstitial inflammation. Benign nephrosclerosis, in contrast, makes both kidneys evenly small with a finely granular surface.
whyNot: Symmetric shrinkage with a fine granular surface is benign nephrosclerosis from long-standing hypertension.
Flea-bitten pinpoint hemorrhages are typical of malignant hypertension.
Correct.
Enlarged, pale kidneys fit diseases that add material or swelling, such as amyloidosis, rather than repeated scarring.

questions.stem: Further imaging shows that her right kidney has two renal pelves whose ureters join at the level of the pelvic brim and enter the bladder through a single orifice. Which of the following developmental events best explains this finding?
options: Early splitting of a single ureteric bud
Two separate ureteric buds from one mesonephric duct
Failure of the ureteric bud to induce the blastema
Incomplete fusion of the paramesonephric ducts
approach: Note the key detail: two pelves but only one ureteral orifice in the bladder.
Recall the two mechanisms: a single bud that divides early gives a bifid (partly duplicated) ureter, while two buds give two complete ureters with two orifices.
Conclude that early splitting of one bud explains a Y-shaped ureter with a single orifice.
questions.why: The ureteric bud grows from the mesonephric duct into the metanephric blastema and forms the ureter, pelvis, calyces, and collecting ducts. If the bud divides early, the result is a bifid ureter that joins before reaching the bladder and opens by one orifice. If two buds arise, there are two complete ureters with two orifices, and one may open at an ectopic site. An ectopic orifice can be obstructed or allow reflux; in a complete duplication, the upper pole ureter is the one usually obstructed and the lower pole ureter the one that refluxes.
whyNot: Correct.
Two separate buds produce a complete duplication with two ureteral orifices in the bladder.
Failed interaction between bud and blastema leads to renal agenesis or dysplasia, not a duplicated collecting system.
The paramesonephric ducts form the uterus and uterine tubes. Incomplete fusion gives a bicornuate uterus.

dx: Benign nephrosclerosis with chronic kidney disease in an older man with long-standing hypertension
case: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician for follow-up of hypertension that was diagnosed 25 years ago and has often been poorly controlled. He does not have diabetes. He reports fatigue. Blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), mean corpuscular volume 88 fL (80 to 100), reticulocyte count 0.4% (0.5 to 1.5), urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL (7 to 20), creatinine 2.5 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3), estimated GFR 25 mL/min/1.73 m2 (over 90), calcium 8.3 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), phosphate 5.4 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), and parathyroid hormone 190 pg/mL (10 to 65). Urine protein is 0.5 g/day (under 0.15), and the sediment is bland. Ultrasonography shows two small kidneys of equal size with thin cortices. Diagnosis: chronic kidney disease from benign nephrosclerosis.

questions.stem: A kidney biopsy specimen from this patient would most likely show which of the following changes in the walls of the afferent arterioles?
options: Concentric onion-skin layering of smooth muscle cells
Fibrinoid necrosis with fragmented red cells
Transmural neutrophils with nuclear debris
Homogeneous pink hyaline thickening
approach: Classify the disease: decades of moderate hypertension with a slowly rising creatinine and symmetric small kidneys is benign nephrosclerosis.
Recall the arteriolar lesion of chronic, moderate pressure: plasma proteins leak into the wall and basement membrane material accumulates.
Conclude: hyaline arteriolosclerosis, a glassy pink thickening that narrows the lumen and causes patchy ischemic atrophy.
questions.why: In benign nephrosclerosis, long-standing hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis: arteriolar walls are thickened by homogeneous, pink, glassy material from leaked plasma proteins and extra matrix. The narrowed lumens cause patchy ischemia, so nephrons drop out and the cortex scars. Grossly, the kidneys are symmetrically small with a finely granular surface. Malignant hypertension instead causes hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis and fibrinoid necrosis, with pinpoint hemorrhages giving a flea-bitten kidney and rapid renal failure.
whyNot: Onion-skin smooth muscle layering is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis of malignant hypertension, with very high pressures and rapid renal failure.
Fibrinoid necrosis with fragmented red cells occurs in malignant hypertension and in thrombotic microangiopathies such as hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Neutrophils with nuclear debris across the wall describe a necrotizing vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa.
Correct.

questions.stem: Serum iron studies, vitamin B12, and folate are normal. Which of the following best explains his anemia?
options: Deficient renal erythropoietin production
Hemolysis of red cells by circulating autoantibodies
Chronic blood loss from glomerular hematuria
Impaired DNA synthesis in marrow precursor cells
approach: Characterize the anemia: normocytic, with a low reticulocyte count, so the marrow is underproducing.
Exclude common nutritional causes: iron, B12, and folate are normal.
Link it to CKD: loss of peritubular interstitial cells reduces erythropoietin, so red cell production falls as GFR declines.
questions.why: Erythropoietin is made by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the renal cortex in response to hypoxia. As chronic kidney disease destroys renal tissue, erythropoietin output falls and the marrow makes fewer red cells, producing a normocytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count. Anemia is one of several predictable consequences of CKD, along with hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, hypertension, renal osteodystrophy, and uremic complications such as pericarditis, encephalopathy, and platelet dysfunction. Diabetes and hypertension are the leading causes of CKD.
whyNot: Correct.
Autoimmune hemolysis raises the reticulocyte count. His marrow response is low.
His urine sediment is bland, and chronic blood loss would cause iron deficiency with microcytosis.
Impaired DNA synthesis from B12 or folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anemia. His MCV and vitamin levels are normal.

questions.stem: Renal autoregulation partly protected his glomeruli during years of high blood pressure. In tubuloglomerular feedback, increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa causes afferent arteriolar constriction. Which of the following signals most directly produces this constriction?
options: Nitric oxide released by macula densa cells
Adenosine acting on A1 receptors
Increased renin secretion by juxtaglomerular cells
Prostaglandin E2 acting on the efferent arteriole
approach: Recall the sensor: macula densa cells in the thick ascending limb take up NaCl through the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter.
Recall the signal: high NaCl uptake leads to release of ATP, which is converted to adenosine.
Apply it: adenosine acts on A1 receptors on the afferent arteriole, constricting it and bringing GFR back toward normal.
questions.why: Autoregulation keeps renal blood flow and GFR fairly constant over a wide range of arterial pressure. The myogenic response constricts the afferent arteriole when its wall is stretched. Tubuloglomerular feedback senses NaCl at the macula densa: when GFR rises, more NaCl arrives, and the macula densa releases ATP and adenosine, which constrict the afferent arteriole through A1 receptors. When NaCl delivery falls, the afferent arteriole dilates and renin release rises. In long-standing hypertension these responses protect the glomeruli only partly, and arteriolosclerosis develops.
whyNot: Nitric oxide from the macula densa is a vasodilator that dampens the feedback response.
Correct.
High NaCl at the macula densa suppresses renin release. Renin rises when NaCl delivery falls.
Prostaglandin E2 is a vasodilator, and a change at the efferent arteriole would not produce afferent constriction.

questions.stem: His 50-year-old brother has normal kidney function and a parathyroid adenoma. Which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely in the brother?
options: Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH
Low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
High calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
approach: Recall PTH actions: it releases calcium from bone, increases distal calcium reabsorption, reduces proximal phosphate reabsorption, and stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
Apply them to autonomous PTH excess with healthy kidneys: calcium rises and phosphate falls.
Contrast with this patient: in CKD, phosphate is retained and calcitriol falls, so calcium is low and PTH rises in response.
questions.why: PTH acts on the proximal tubule to inhibit phosphate reabsorption and to stimulate 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which makes calcitriol (low phosphate also stimulates this enzyme). In primary hyperparathyroidism with healthy kidneys, PTH is high, calcium is high, and phosphate is low. In chronic kidney disease, failing kidneys retain phosphate and make little calcitriol, so calcium falls and PTH rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism). Vitamin D deficiency gives low calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH. Severe hypomagnesemia causes hypocalcemia that resists treatment, because magnesium is needed for PTH release and action.
whyNot: Low calcium, high phosphate, and high PTH is the secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic kidney disease, the pattern in this patient.
Low calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH fits vitamin D deficiency, where PTH rises to defend calcium and wastes phosphate.
Correct.
High calcium and phosphate with suppressed PTH suggests vitamin D excess or another PTH-independent cause of hypercalcemia.

dx: Cauda equina syndrome with a flaccid overflow bladder and Klebsiella cystitis
case: A 51-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of severe low back pain, weakness of both legs, and inability to urinate for 2 days. Temperature is 37.3 °C (99.1 °F), pulse 92/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg. Examination shows a palpable, nontender bladder, reduced sensation over the perineum and buttocks, weak ankle plantar flexion on both sides, absent ankle reflexes, and reduced anal sphincter tone. Bladder catheterization drains 1,300 mL of urine. MRI shows a large central L4 to L5 disc herniation compressing the cauda equina. On the third day of catheter drainage her urine becomes cloudy. Urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite, and culture grows more than 100,000 CFU/mL of Klebsiella pneumoniae. Diagnosis: cauda equina syndrome with a flaccid overflow bladder and Klebsiella cystitis.

questions.stem: Loss of which of the following pathways most directly explains why her detrusor fails to contract?
options: Pelvic splanchnic parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4
Hypogastric sympathetic fibers from T11 to L2
Pudendal somatic fibers to the external sphincter
Reticulospinal fibers from the pontine micturition center
approach: Localize the lesion: cauda equina compression damages the sacral roots S2 to S4.
Recall which pathway contracts the detrusor: parasympathetic fibers in the pelvic splanchnic nerves, acting on muscarinic receptors.
Predict the bladder: without this efferent limb and its sensory input, the detrusor is flaccid, the bladder overfills, and urine leaks as overflow.
questions.why: Micturition is a spinal reflex at S2 to S4 that the pontine micturition center coordinates. Bladder stretch signals travel in pelvic nerves to the sacral cord, and parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic fibers return to contract the detrusor. Sympathetic hypogastric fibers relax the detrusor and contract the internal sphincter during filling, and pudendal fibers keep the external sphincter closed. A lesion of the sacral cord or cauda equina breaks the reflex arc, giving a flaccid, large-capacity bladder with overflow. A lesion above the sacral cord leaves the arc intact, giving a small, spastic reflex bladder that may contract against a closed sphincter.
whyNot: Correct.
Sympathetic hypogastric fibers relax the detrusor and close the bladder neck during filling. Their loss would not prevent contraction.
Pudendal fibers control the external sphincter. Their loss adds to incontinence but does not stop the detrusor from contracting.
Loss of pontine input, as with a cord lesion above the sacral segments, leaves the sacral reflex intact and causes a spastic bladder.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures of the organism isolated from her urine gives its colonies a mucoid appearance and helps it resist phagocytosis?
options: Teichoic acid
Type 1 fimbriae
Polysaccharide capsule
Peritrichous swarming flagella
approach: Identify the organism: Klebsiella pneumoniae, a nonmotile, lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod that thrives with urinary retention and catheters.
Recall its signature virulence factor: a thick polysaccharide capsule.
Link structure to findings: the capsule makes colonies mucoid and blocks phagocytosis and complement.
questions.why: Klebsiella pneumoniae is an encapsulated, nonmotile, lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. Its thick polysaccharide capsule makes colonies large and mucoid and protects the bacteria from phagocytosis. It causes urinary infections, especially with catheters, diabetes, or urinary retention, and also pneumonia. Other urinary pathogens to know are Escherichia coli (most common), Staphylococcus saprophyticus (coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant, in young sexually active women), Enterococcus, Proteus, and Pseudomonas (catheter-associated).
whyNot: Teichoic acid is a cell wall component of gram-positive bacteria. Klebsiella is gram-negative.
Type 1 fimbriae help bacteria such as E. coli stick to bladder cells, but they do not make colonies mucoid.
Correct.
Peritrichous flagella with swarming motility belong to Proteus. Klebsiella is nonmotile.

questions.stem: If her bladder is left undrained, she is most likely to leak small amounts of urine almost constantly. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this type of incontinence?
options: Involuntary detrusor contractions during bladder filling
Urethral hypermobility from weak pelvic floor support
Reflex detrusor contraction against a closed sphincter
Passive leakage from an overfilled, flaccid bladder
approach: Note the bladder: flaccid and overfilled, because the detrusor cannot contract.
Recall overflow incontinence: once bladder pressure exceeds urethral resistance, urine dribbles out passively, with a large residual volume.
Separate it from stress incontinence (weak urethral support, leaks with cough) and urge incontinence (detrusor overactivity).
questions.why: Overflow incontinence occurs when the bladder cannot empty, either because the detrusor is underactive, as with sacral or cauda equina lesions or diabetic neuropathy, or because the outlet is obstructed, as with prostatic enlargement. The bladder fills until its pressure exceeds outlet resistance, then urine dribbles out, and a large volume remains after voiding. Stress incontinence results from weak pelvic floor and urethral support, often after vaginal deliveries, and causes leaks with coughing or lifting. Urge incontinence results from involuntary detrusor contractions.
whyNot: Involuntary detrusor contractions cause urge incontinence, with sudden urgency. Her detrusor cannot contract at all.
Weak urethral support causes stress incontinence, with leaks during coughing, sneezing, or lifting and a small residual volume.
Reflex contraction against a closed sphincter (dyssynergia) occurs with spinal lesions above the sacral cord, not with cauda equina compression.
Correct.

questions.stem: Compared with a histologic section of an empty bladder, a section of her bladder wall fixed while severely distended would most likely show which of the following?
options: Many layers with dome-shaped surface cells
Few layers of flattened surface cells
Stratified squamous cells with surface keratin
Simple columnar cells with goblet cells
approach: Recall that the bladder lining is urothelium (transitional epithelium) with large surface umbrella cells.
Recall how it accommodates filling: cells flatten and slide past each other, and umbrella cells add stored membrane to their surface.
Predict the distended appearance: a thin lining of a few layers with flat surface cells, while the barrier stays intact.
questions.why: The empty bladder has a thick urothelium with several cell layers and large, dome-shaped umbrella cells. As the bladder fills, cells flatten and rearrange, so the lining looks only a few layers thick, and umbrella cells enlarge their apical surface by inserting stored membrane vesicles. Tight junctions and uroplakin plaques keep urine from leaking into the wall. Beneath the urothelium lie the lamina propria and the detrusor smooth muscle, which in her case is overstretched and not contracting.
whyNot: Many layers with dome-shaped surface cells is the appearance of the empty, relaxed bladder.
Correct.
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium appears only after squamous metaplasia from chronic irritation, such as long-term catheters or schistosomiasis.
Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells is an intestinal-type lining, seen in the bladder only with glandular metaplasia or urachal remnants.

dx: Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis with reactive arthritis in a young man
case: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of a painful, swollen right knee and left ankle for 5 days and red, irritated eyes for 3 days. Three weeks ago, after sex with a new partner, he had mild burning on urination and a scant, watery urethral discharge that faded without treatment. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). Examination shows conjunctival injection of both eyes, a warm knee effusion, a swollen left ankle, and tenderness at the left Achilles tendon insertion. Synovial fluid shows 18,000 leukocytes/mm3, mostly neutrophils, no crystals, and a negative Gram stain and culture. Nucleic acid amplification testing of first-void urine is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. HLA-B27 is positive. Diagnosis: Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis with reactive arthritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following forms of the organism was transmitted to him and entered his urethral epithelial cells?
options: Reticulate body
Endospore
Elementary body
Trophozoite
approach: Identify the organism: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K, an obligate intracellular bacterium.
Recall its two forms: the small, hardy elementary body is infectious and enters cells by endocytosis; inside, it becomes the reticulate body, which divides.
Conclude that the transmitted form is the elementary body.
questions.why: Chlamydia trachomatis depends on host cell ATP and grows only inside host cells. The elementary body is small, metabolically inactive, and survives outside cells; it attaches to columnar epithelium and is taken in by endocytosis. Inside the inclusion it reorganizes into the larger reticulate body, which divides by binary fission and then condenses back into elementary bodies that are released to infect new cells. Serovars D to K cause urethritis, cervicitis, and conjunctivitis. Nucleic acid amplification testing is the diagnostic test for both Chlamydia and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
whyNot: The reticulate body is the replicating form inside the inclusion. It is fragile and not infectious outside the cell.
Endospores are made by some gram-positive rods such as Clostridium and Bacillus. Chlamydia does not form spores.
Correct.
Trophozoites are the active forms of protozoa such as Trichomonas vaginalis, which can also cause urethritis but is not a bacterium.

questions.stem: A Gram stain of his urethral discharge, had it been obtained 3 weeks ago, would most likely have shown which of the following?
options: Gram-positive cocci in clusters
Clue cells covered with gram-variable rods
Neutrophils with intracellular gram-negative diplococci
Neutrophils without visible organisms
approach: Note the clinical type: scant, watery discharge with mild dysuria and a positive Chlamydia test point to nongonococcal urethritis.
Recall that Chlamydia lives inside cells and is not seen on Gram stain.
Predict neutrophils without organisms, while gonococcal urethritis shows gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils with a purulent discharge.
questions.why: Gonococcal urethritis usually causes a heavy, purulent discharge, and Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils. Nongonococcal urethritis, most often from Chlamydia trachomatis, causes milder dysuria and a scant, clear discharge; Gram stain shows neutrophils but no bacteria. Both can lead to epididymitis in men and pelvic inflammatory disease in women. Chlamydia is also the classic trigger of reactive arthritis, a sterile, immune-mediated arthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis that is strongly linked to HLA-B27, as in this patient.
whyNot: Gram-positive cocci in clusters suggest Staphylococcus. S. saprophyticus causes cystitis rather than urethral discharge.
Clue cells with gram-variable rods are the finding of bacterial vaginosis from Gardnerella in women.
Neutrophils with intracellular gram-negative diplococci are the finding of gonococcal urethritis, which usually causes a purulent discharge.
Correct.

questions.stem: A swab inserted 2 to 3 cm into the external urethral meatus samples the epithelium of which of the following segments of the male urethra?
options: Spongy urethra
Membranous urethra
Prostatic urethra
Intramural (preprostatic) urethra
approach: Recall the segments of the male urethra from bladder to meatus: intramural, prostatic, membranous, and spongy.
Recall their lengths: the spongy urethra is the longest, about 15 cm, running through the corpus spongiosum of the penis to the meatus.
Conclude that the first few centimeters from the meatus are spongy urethra, the site usually sampled in urethritis.
questions.why: The male urethra is about 18 to 22 cm long. It begins at the internal urethral orifice at the apex of the trigone, runs through the prostate (prostatic urethra, which receives the ejaculatory and prostatic ducts), passes through the external urethral sphincter (membranous urethra, the narrowest and least distensible part), and then travels through the corpus spongiosum (spongy urethra) to the external meatus. The female urethra is only about 4 cm long and opens just in front of the vagina, which is why women have far more ascending bladder infections.
whyNot: Correct.
The membranous urethra lies deep in the perineum, about 15 cm from the meatus, where it passes through the external urethral sphincter.
The prostatic urethra lies within the prostate just below the bladder, far beyond the reach of a short swab.
The intramural urethra lies within the bladder neck and is the deepest segment.

questions.stem: Dipstick testing of his first-void urine 3 weeks ago would most likely have shown which of the following results?
options: Leukocyte esterase negative, nitrite positive
Leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative
Leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite positive
Leukocyte esterase negative, nitrite negative
approach: Leukocyte esterase marks neutrophils, which fill the urethra in urethritis.
Nitrite requires bacteria with nitrate reductase, mainly Enterobacterales such as E. coli, multiplying in the bladder.
Chlamydia does not reduce nitrate, so the expected pattern is pyuria with a negative nitrite and no growth on routine culture (sterile pyuria).
questions.why: Leukocyte esterase is an enzyme released by neutrophils, so a positive result means pyuria. A positive nitrite means gram-negative bacteria with nitrate reductase have converted urinary nitrate, as in E. coli cystitis. In chlamydial urethritis, first-void urine contains neutrophils from the urethra but no nitrate-reducing bacteria, and routine cultures are negative. This sterile pyuria suggests urethritis, renal tuberculosis, or interstitial nephritis. White cell casts would instead place the inflammation in the kidney.
whyNot: A positive nitrite with a negative esterase suggests bacteriuria with little inflammation, and Chlamydia does not produce nitrite.
Correct.
Both tests positive is the usual pattern of E. coli cystitis. Chlamydia does not reduce nitrate.
His urethra is inflamed, so neutrophils in first-void urine should give a positive esterase.

dx: AA amyloidosis with nephrotic syndrome and renal vein thrombosis in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis
case: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 4 months of leg swelling and foamy urine. She has had rheumatoid arthritis for 25 years with persistent active synovitis despite treatment. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Examination shows pitting edema to the thighs and ulnar deviation of both hands. Laboratory studies show serum albumin 1.8 g/dL (3.5 to 5.0), total cholesterol 352 mg/dL (under 200), creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), C-reactive protein 46 mg/L (under 5), and urine protein 8.6 g/day (under 0.15). Kidney biopsy shows glomerular deposits with apple-green birefringence after Congo red staining that react with antibody to serum amyloid A. Two weeks later she has sudden left flank pain and gross hematuria, and Doppler ultrasonography shows a thrombus in the left renal vein. Diagnosis: AA amyloidosis with nephrotic syndrome and renal vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: The precursor of these amyloid deposits is produced mainly by which of the following cells, in response to which stimulus?
options: Plasma cells, in response to clonal expansion
Hepatocytes, in response to IL-6 and IL-1
Macrophages, in response to immune complexes
Tubular cells, in response to filtered protein
approach: Identify the amyloid type: deposits reacting with serum amyloid A in a patient with long-standing inflammation are AA amyloid.
Recall that serum amyloid A is an acute phase protein.
Recall the source: hepatocytes make acute phase proteins when stimulated by IL-6, IL-1, and TNF from activated macrophages.
questions.why: AA amyloid comes from serum amyloid A, an acute phase protein made by the liver in response to cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1. Chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and chronic infections keep its level high, and its fragments misfold into beta-pleated sheet fibrils. AL amyloid instead comes from monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains made by plasma cells. Both types bind Congo red and show apple-green birefringence under polarized light. In the kidney, amyloid deposits in the mesangium and capillary walls and causes heavy proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot: Clonal plasma cells make immunoglobulin light chains, the precursor of AL amyloid seen in myeloma and primary amyloidosis.
Correct.
Macrophages release the cytokines that drive serum amyloid A production, but they do not make the precursor protein themselves.
Tubular cells reabsorb filtered protein but do not produce amyloid precursors.

questions.stem: Among adults with nephrotic syndrome, this vascular complication is most strongly associated with which of the following glomerular diseases?
options: Membranous nephropathy
Minimal change disease
IgA nephropathy
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
approach: Recall why nephrotic syndrome promotes clotting: urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins and increased hepatic production of clotting factors.
Recall which nephrotic disease carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis: membranous nephropathy.
Set aside the nephritic diseases, which do not cause this degree of protein loss.
questions.why: Renal vein thrombosis causes flank pain, hematuria, and an enlarged, swollen kidney, sometimes with worsening kidney function. Its main causes are nephrotic syndrome, renal cell carcinoma growing into the renal vein, and severe dehydration in infants. Among nephrotic diseases, membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk. The hypercoagulable state comes from urinary loss of antithrombin III and other anticoagulant proteins, together with increased hepatic production of fibrinogen and other clotting factors.
whyNot: Correct.
Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome with some clotting risk, but renal vein thrombosis is much more typical of membranous nephropathy.
IgA nephropathy usually presents with hematuria and modest proteinuria, without the heavy protein loss that drives clotting.
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a nephritic syndrome with modest proteinuria.

questions.stem: In addition to increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis, which of the following most likely contributes to her hypercholesterolemia?
options: Increased intestinal absorption of dietary cholesterol
Urinary loss of LDL particles through the damaged filter
Increased LDL receptor activity in hepatocytes
Reduced catabolism of circulating lipoproteins
approach: Recall the two sides of nephrotic hyperlipidemia: more lipoprotein made by the liver and less removed from the blood.
Recall the removal defects: lower lipoprotein lipase activity slows VLDL breakdown, and hepatic uptake of LDL falls.
Conclude that reduced catabolism adds to increased synthesis to raise cholesterol.
questions.why: In nephrotic syndrome the liver responds to low plasma oncotic pressure by making more lipoproteins, including apolipoprotein B-containing particles. At the same time, lipoproteins are cleared more slowly, because lipoprotein lipase activity falls and hepatic LDL uptake is reduced. The result is high cholesterol and often high triglycerides. Lipid also leaks into the urine (lipiduria), where it appears as oval fat bodies and fatty casts that show Maltese crosses under polarized light.
whyNot: Dietary absorption is not increased in nephrotic syndrome. The problem is hepatic overproduction and impaired clearance.
LDL particles are too large to cross even a damaged glomerular filter in large amounts, and losing them would lower cholesterol.
Greater LDL receptor activity would clear more LDL from the blood and lower cholesterol. In nephrotic syndrome, hepatic LDL uptake is reduced.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, which of the following urine sediment findings would have been most consistent with her syndrome?
options: Red cell casts with dysmorphic red cells
Muddy brown granular casts
Fatty casts with few red cells
White cell casts with bacteria
approach: Classify the syndrome: proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, low albumin, edema, and high cholesterol define nephrotic syndrome.
Recall the matching sediment: lipid in the urine forms fatty casts and oval fat bodies, with little blood.
Contrast nephritic syndrome, which shows hematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, oliguria, and azotemia.
questions.why: Nephrotic syndrome results from damage to the filtration barrier that lets large amounts of protein through: proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria with fatty casts. The sediment is usually bland apart from lipid. Nephritic syndrome results from glomerular inflammation: hematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, oliguria, azotemia, and proteinuria under 3.5 g/day. Amyloidosis, membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and diabetic nephropathy typically present as nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot: Red cell casts with dysmorphic red cells mark glomerular inflammation, the hallmark of nephritic syndrome.
Muddy brown granular casts are shed tubular cells in acute tubular necrosis.
Correct.
White cell casts with bacteria indicate acute pyelonephritis.

dx: Papillary renal cell carcinoma arising in acquired cystic kidney disease in a long-term dialysis patient
case: A 58-year-old man who has received hemodialysis for 14 years for end-stage renal disease from IgA nephropathy comes to the physician because of two episodes of visible blood in his small daily urine output. He has lost 4 kg (9 lb) over 3 months. Hemoglobin is 10.9 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5) while he receives erythropoietin therapy. He has no family history of kidney disease. CT shows two small kidneys containing many cortical cysts of varying size and a 3.5-cm solid, enhancing mass in the upper pole of the left kidney. A left nephrectomy is performed, and pathologic examination shows renal cell carcinoma of the papillary type arising among multiple cysts. Diagnosis: papillary renal cell carcinoma in acquired cystic kidney disease.

questions.stem: Cytogenetic analysis of the tumor shows trisomy of chromosomes 7 and 17. The extra copy of chromosome 7 most likely contributes to tumor growth through increased dosage of which of the following genes?
options: VHL, a tumor suppressor that targets HIF for degradation
WT1, a transcription factor in nephron development
RET, a receptor tyrosine kinase of neural crest cells
MET, the hepatocyte growth factor receptor
approach: Recognize the cytogenetic pattern: trisomies 7 and 17 are typical of papillary renal cell carcinoma.
Recall the oncogene on chromosome 7 linked to this tumor: MET, which encodes the receptor tyrosine kinase for hepatocyte growth factor.
Apply it: extra copies, or activating mutations in hereditary papillary carcinoma, increase MET signaling and drive proliferation.
questions.why: Papillary renal cell carcinoma is the second most common type and is frequent in acquired cystic disease of dialysis. It typically shows trisomies 7 and 17 and, in men, loss of the Y chromosome. MET, on chromosome 7, encodes the receptor tyrosine kinase for hepatocyte growth factor; gains of chromosome 7 raise its dosage, and germline activating MET mutations cause hereditary papillary renal carcinoma. Microscopically the tumor forms papillae with foamy macrophages in their cores. Clear cell carcinoma instead loses VHL on chromosome 3p, chromophobe carcinoma arises from intercalated cells, and oncocytoma is a benign tumor packed with mitochondria.
whyNot: VHL on chromosome 3p is a tumor suppressor that is lost in clear cell carcinoma. Extra copies would not promote growth.
WT1 on chromosome 11p is a tumor suppressor that is lost in some Wilms tumors.
RET on chromosome 10 is activated in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 and medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the origin of the cysts in his kidneys?
options: Biallelic PKHD1 mutations affecting ciliary fibrocystin
Germline PKD1 mutation with a second somatic hit
Acquired tubular dilation in scarred end-stage kidneys
Abnormal metanephric differentiation in fetal life
approach: Note the setting: small, scarred kidneys after many years of dialysis, no family history, and cysts that appeared late in life.
Recall that acquired cystic disease develops in end-stage kidneys from any cause, with cysts thought to arise from tubules blocked by scarring or crystals.
Distinguish it from inherited autosomal dominant and recessive PKD and from multicystic dysplasia present at birth.
questions.why: Acquired cystic kidney disease develops in end-stage kidneys, especially after years of dialysis, whatever the original kidney disease. The kidneys are usually small or normal in size, and the cysts are thought to arise from tubules blocked by interstitial scarring or crystals. Its main danger is renal cell carcinoma, often papillary, which is much more common than in the general population. Autosomal recessive PKD presents in infancy with huge kidneys, Potter sequence, and congenital hepatic fibrosis. Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a sporadic, usually unilateral malformation present at birth.
whyNot: PKHD1 mutations cause autosomal recessive PKD, which presents in infancy with large kidneys and hepatic fibrosis.
A germline PKD1 mutation causes autosomal dominant PKD, with large cystic kidneys and usually a family history.
Correct.
Abnormal metanephric differentiation causes multicystic dysplastic kidney, which is present at birth and usually affects one side.

questions.stem: In the clear cell type of renal cell carcinoma, the most common type overall, the tumor cells look empty on routine sections. Which of the following best explains this appearance?
options: Lipid and glycogen removed in processing
Mitochondria packed throughout the cytoplasm
Mucin vacuoles pushing the nucleus aside
Hydropic swelling from ischemic injury
approach: Recall the origin of clear cell carcinoma: proximal tubule cells that store abundant lipid and glycogen.
Recall what routine processing does: solvents dissolve lipid and glycogen is lost from the sections, leaving empty-looking cytoplasm.
Connect: the same stored lipid gives the tumor its golden-yellow cut surface.
questions.why: Clear cell carcinoma is the most common renal cancer and arises from proximal tubule epithelium. Its cells are filled with lipid and glycogen, which wash out during routine tissue processing, so the cytoplasm looks clear. Grossly the tumor is golden yellow. Risk factors include smoking, obesity, hypertension, and acquired cystic disease of dialysis, and the tumor tends to grow into the renal vein and then the inferior vena cava, spreading through the blood to the lungs and bones.
whyNot: Correct.
Cytoplasm packed with mitochondria is pink and granular, the pattern of oncocytoma, a benign tumor.
Mucin vacuoles that push the nucleus aside produce signet ring cells, as in some gastric adenocarcinomas.
Hydropic swelling is a reversible injury change with pale cytoplasm. It does not explain the stored lipid and glycogen of a carcinoma.

questions.stem: During the nephrectomy, the surgeon finds that the tumor at the upper pole has grown through the renal fascia on the anterolateral surface. Which of the following organs is most at risk of direct invasion at this site?
options: Right lobe of the liver
Spleen
Descending part of the duodenum
Right colic flexure
approach: Note the site: the anterolateral surface of the upper pole of the left kidney.
Recall the anterior relations of the left kidney: stomach and spleen above, pancreatic tail in the middle, and jejunum and left colic flexure below.
Conclude that the spleen lies against the upper lateral part, so it is at risk.
questions.why: The anterior surface of the left kidney touches the stomach and spleen superiorly, the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels near the middle, and the jejunum and left colic flexure inferiorly, and the suprarenal gland sits on the upper pole medially. The right kidney lies against the liver, the descending duodenum near its hilum, and the right colic flexure below. A tumor breaking out of the upper lateral left kidney can therefore reach the spleen.
whyNot: The right lobe of the liver lies in front of the right kidney, on the opposite side.
Correct.
The descending duodenum lies in front of the right renal hilum.
The right colic flexure lies in front of the lower pole of the right kidney.
